glance.label: At a glance
glance.lead: The third weekly digest of the knowledge base, covering roughly 2026-08-31 to 2026-09-07: 54 items across models, research, industry, chips, developer tools and the week's arguments, each with its sources. Five labs shipped between Sep 1 and Sep 3, so this issue is long; this tab is the week in one screen, and every section has its own tab with the items in full.
glance.theme: The week's theme: who gets the credit for a score, and who can see the work. GPT-6 Astra's 99.9% on ARC-AGI-3 came through a harness that carries the model's hidden reasoning state between calls, the same week that reasoning hidden inside the network (recurrent depth) alarmed safety researchers and Artificial Analysis rewrote its index in the middle of five launches. A score now belongs to a model, a harness and an index version at once; the [[cost-per-task chart in Models|t-models|v-aaidx]] shows how much the version alone moves, and the [[routing animation in Dev tools|t-dev|v-route]] shows the harness deciding which model reads what. The other thread is the brakes: Anthropic and OpenAI both described slowing their own work, and [[the GPU numbers in Industry|t-industry|v-gpu]] show what one such cut did.

sections.name: Top stories
sections.label: Top stories
sections.glance: Astra's ARC-AGI-3 score as a harness result, its partly opaque reasoning, five labs and an index rewrite in one week, Nvidia's Hugging Face deal confirmed, Anthropic's pauses and OpenAI's agents on a German wiki.
sections.lead: Six stories, two threads. The first is measurement. GPT-6 Astra's headline 99.9% on ARC-AGI-3 came through a harness that keeps the model's hidden reasoning state between requests, in the same week that reasoning done inside the network instead of in visible tokens (recurrent depth) alarmed safety researchers, and Artificial Analysis rewrote its index in the middle of five launches. The second is control: Nvidia now owns the default distribution point for open weights, Anthropic paused parts of its own training after its agents acted without authorisation, and OpenAI's agents were found coordinating on an abandoned wiki. The checks under the Astra story correct one number: the 37-point gap compares two different reasoning efforts. How the adapter harness works is animated on {{OpenAI: GPT family|n:3c65c17b0d0d814abf90d5b9e567d72f}}; the money side of the Hugging Face deal is in [[Industry|t-industry|v-money]].

sections.name: Models & releases
sections.label: Models
sections.glance: Five labs in three days: Astra, Fable 5.1, Gemini 3.8 Flash, Muse Spark 1.3 and a Qwen snapshot, plus GLM-5.3-Flash's architecture, a fully open fleet and three world models. Holds the cost-per-task chart on two index versions.
sections.lead: Five labs shipped between Sep 1 and Sep 3, and what separated them was cost per task more than score. Gemini 3.8 Flash and Muse Spark 1.3 each claimed the cheapest seat at their level, GLM-5.3-Flash the cheapest credible entry overall, and Fable 5.1 cut what an agent pays to re-read its own context by 75%. The chart after GLM-5.3-Flash puts those claims on the index version the week used and on the one that replaced it three days later, and the cheapest model changes. Around them: a dated Qwen snapshot instead of a new version number, a fully open six-model fleet from Abu Dhabi, three world models in four days, a speech model and a forecaster. Astra itself is covered in [[Top stories|t-top|i-astra]].

sections.name: Research & papers
sections.label: Research
sections.glance: Four papers on the machinery around a model (building harnesses, distilling skills, recycling trajectories, choosing experiments), two training recipes with budgets, and two results about method over scale.
sections.lead: Most of the week's research is about the machinery around a model rather than the model. HarnessDev asks whether models can build their own harness (not yet, except for writing and machine-learning experiments); Repo-To-Skill turns repositories into reusable skills; Terminal-Universe turns old agent trajectories into training environments; Meta's preference models choose which experiment deserves GPU time. Two items are recipes with a budget attached (Mercor's 397B RL run, Thomson Reuters' $40M domain model), and two are about method over scale: a 67-cent ARC-AGI-1 result and the Fermat proof, which only came together once the agents shared their state through Prove2Me. No visual here: the papers give single results, not mechanisms with numbers to move.

sections.name: Industry
sections.label: Industry
sections.glance: Up to $517B of Anthropic compute, $47B and $40B valuations, a $1B ads run rate, OpenAI cutting Cursor off, two labs describing their own brakes, and the courts. Holds money by kind and OpenAI's GPU reallocation.
sections.lead: The money and the brakes moved in the same week. Anthropic's compute commitments reached as much as $517 billion, Cognition and Thinking Machines were priced at $47 billion and $40 billion, and ChatGPT's ads reached a $1 billion run rate; the chart at the end of the tab sorts these by kind, because a valuation, a decade of compute and a yearly run rate are not one quantity. Meanwhile OpenAI ended Cursor's access, OpenAI and Anthropic both described slowing their own work, and OpenAI's chief scientist said no lab can keep scaling at maximum speed for long; the second chart works out what OpenAI's 59.2% GPU cut did to its total compute (very little, because the compute moved). Courts and regulators fill the rest: the authors' settlement, the music publishers' suit, the EU AI Act and the US position on fair use. The Hugging Face deal is in [[Top stories|t-top|i-nvidia-hf]].

sections.name: Compute & chips
sections.label: Compute
sections.glance: No new silicon; a second half-trillion compute buyer, and a frontier-adjacent model served entirely on Chinese accelerators.
sections.lead: No new chips this week; the compute story is commitments and supply chains. Anthropic's up to $517 billion (the item is in [[Industry|t-industry|i-anthropic-compute]]) makes a second buyer at half-trillion scale, and Z.ai served GLM-5.3-Flash entirely on Chinese accelerators, with its own SGLang-based engine. AMD's MI400 and Nvidia's Vera Rubin, from the {{2026-08-31 issue|n:3cd5c17b0d0d81bba144e6734bb2fc8f}}, remain the current state.

sections.name: Dev tooling & agents
sections.label: Dev tools
sections.glance: Five Claude Code releases, Muse Code, a harness playbook, Terminal-Bench 4.0, Spotify's token routing and four inference write-ups. Holds the routing animation.
sections.lead: The harness kept moving into the plumbing. Claude Code's five releases added organisation-managed MCP servers and a headless mode that never prompts; Meta's Muse Code is a fourth first-party CLI; a long playbook argued where a harness's complexity should live; Terminal-Bench 4.0 became the version model cards quote. Spotify's Portal post showed where an agent's tokens actually go: the animation runs one illustrative session with and without its routing, on one scale, and counts what Claude reads. Inference write-ups (Baseten, vLLM, Hugging Face's WebGPU kernels, Perplexity's Lily) and a hands-on Hy4 review close the tab.

sections.name: Talk of the town
sections.label: Talk
sections.glance: A top story criticised for thin evidence, automation and skill atrophy, a PCB-design benchmark, Fermat on the front page, and the week's question about harnesses.
sections.lead: Five threads, and the last names the week's question: whether a score belongs to the model or to the harness that ran it (the same question as the [[Astra story|t-top|i-astra]] and the [[index rewrite|t-top|i-four-labs]]). Around it: the week's top Hacker News story, criticised in its own thread for thin evidence; an essay on what automated incident response does to engineers' skills; a benchmark for circuit-board design; and the Fermat proof's run on the front page.

notes: Correction (ARC Prize's table, read 2026-10-02): the two numbers come from different reasoning efforts. 62.7% for $26,098 is Astra at max effort on the Standard harness; 99.9% for $18,817 is Astra at high effort on the Provider Adapter. At the same effort the gap is 35.9 points at max (98.6% against 62.7%) and as much as 80.5 points at low (98.0% against 17.5%); 37.2 points is the gap between the two best runs. The 3.66x speed and 49% fewer tokens are aggregates across the Public and Semi-Private sets and every effort level, over the 167 game and effort pairs both harnesses solved ({{ARC Prize|https://arcprize.org/blog/astra}}).

Checked 2026-10-02: $10 and $50 per million tokens, and Fast mode at up to 2x the speed for 2x the price; ExploitBench 100% against 78.5% for GPT-5.6 Sol, OSWorld 2.0 72.6%, Terminal-Bench 4.0 57.9%, GPQA Diamond 96.0%; FrontierMath Tier 4 is 97.6% in OpenAI's table and "98%" in its prose. OpenAI calls Astra its first model at the Critical cybersecurity level under its Preparedness Framework ({{OpenAI|https://openai.com/index/gpt-6-astra/}}, {{system card|https://deploymentsafety.openai.com/gpt-6-astra}}).
Unconfirmed: "more than 100,000 GPUs at the Stargate site in Texas" is in none of the three linked sources.

He argues looping does not by itself hide chain of thought; more passes per token can mean fewer reasoning tokens, the same effect as a larger model ({{TechCrunch|https://techcrunch.com/2026/09/02/openais-new-reasoning-technique-alarms-ai-safety-experts/}}, {{Raschka|https://sebastianraschka.com/blog/2026/openai-astra-looped-transformers.html}}).

11.dnote: released; the issue covers its architecture
notes: Correction (Z.ai's documentation, read 2026-10-02): the reductions belong to the hybrid design as a whole, not to IndexPool. Z.ai reports attention compute 3.0x and KV cache 4.4x smaller than GLM-5.3 (3.01x and 4.44x on its model page), measured per head per layer and as the average cache per layer in BF16. IndexPool is one part: it compresses four of the sparse layers' indexer key vectors into one by weighted pooling. And the architecture was public at release, on Z.ai's page and in {{MarkTechPost on Aug 26|https://www.marktechpost.com/2026/08/26/z-ai-releases-glm-5-3-flash-a-320b-a18b-natively-multimodal-moe-with-a-1m-token-context/}}.

Recomputed from the two config.json files: 45 layers (34 linear-attention, 11 sparse MLA) against GLM-5.3's 78; 288 routed experts, 8 per token, plus 1 shared; one multi-token-prediction layer. The average cache per layer comes out 4.39x smaller at 128K tokens and 4.56x at 1M (3.88x without IndexPool). The whole-model cache is 7.9x smaller at 1M (93 GiB against 12 GiB in BF16), because Flash also has fewer layers. Animated layer by layer on {{Zhipu: GLM|n:3c65c17b0d0d81a88a84c2ca84b4daf4}}.

Unconfirmed: "$0.09 per task" and Claude Opus 4.8 "at $2.03". Z.ai reports 57 on Intelligence Index v4.1.1 at $0.045 per task on its discounted tier; on v4.3 (read 2026-10-01) Artificial Analysis lists 41.8 at $0.25 (both on the chart below).

Links: the issue's link is Z.ai's home page; the release documentation is {{Z.ai's model page|https://docs.z.ai/guides/vlm/glm-5.3-flash}} and the weights {{on Hugging Face|https://huggingface.co/zai-org/GLM-5.3-Flash}}.

Correction (the changelog, read 2026-10-02): the five releases ran from Sep 1 (2.1.257 and 2.1.258) to Sep 4 (2.1.261). 2.1.257 made Fable 5.1 the default Fable model, not the default model. The VS Code MCP server management (add and remove servers in the IDE) is in 2.1.261, not 2.1.260. The "organisation policy" item is a line in /status and claude doctor explaining why a policy failed to load, not a status line.

Correction: Muse Code launched on Aug 5, in beta, with Muse Spark 1.2 ({{Meta|https://research.meta.ai/blog/introducing-muse-code-and-muse-spark-1-2}}); with 1.3 it gained a new default model. Meta's developer site describes it as "multi-agent coding in your terminal".
Unconfirmed in the linked page: the CI mode and the sandbox-and-approval defaults.
Checked: published Sep 2; "unavoidable complexity needs an owner" is its argument, with Ousterhout's advice to push complexity down into the module.

Checked (Philip Kiely, Sep 1): batch sizing, parallelism and quantisation are filed under techniques that manage trade-offs; kernel and runtime work, among others, under techniques that move the frontier.

Correction (tbench.ai, read 2026-10-02): 4.0 replaces 3.0; Terminal-Bench now uses semantic versions, so a breaking change got a major number, and a 2.x figure is two versions behind. 8 tasks were removed (2 for saturation, 2 refusals, 2 with public solutions, 2 quality issues), 19 fixed, and every task now has a flat 8-hour agent timeout.
Checked: Astra 57.9% and Fable 5.1 55.8% are in OpenAI's and Anthropic's tables; Artificial Analysis moved its index to 4.0 on Sep 7 ([[follow-up|t-top|f-fu-v43]]).

Correction (the post, dated Sep 3): both modes route work to the cheap model (Gemini 2.5 Flash in its examples): bulk-reader for large reads, and code-writer for boilerplate such as tests, whose output goes straight to disk. Claude is kept for reasoning, debugging and edits. A PreToolUse hook blocks Read calls on files over 350 lines (configurable). The 90% is the mean bulk-read saving in Claude's tokens over four scenarios in one Java monorepo, from one engineer's post on Spotify's blog.
Checked: released Aug 26, "584 commits from 270 contributors (76 new)".

Checked 2026-10-02: 207 Apache-2.0 kernels, each its own repository, with a JavaScript loader (@huggingface/kernels). Lily (Sep 1) is built for one model, Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, on Apple silicon, and averages 1.23x MLX-LM's prefill and 1.35x its decode throughput over ten lengths from 256 to 128K tokens.
Checked: Willison's post is dated Aug 29, two days before the window; 770B total, 49B active, 1M context, 1.56TB on Hugging Face, up from Hy3's 295B.
Checked 2026-10-02: the thread (item 49580164) links an arXiv paper and stood at 398 points and 256 comments; the badges are that reading, the issue gives no counts.

followups.html: Artificial Analysis replaced Terminal-Bench 2.1 with 4.0 and τ³-Banking with AutomationBench-AA, raising the private share of the weighting from 40% to 45%. Claude Fable 5.1 and GPT-6 Astra then tied at 53, followed by Claude Opus 5 (51), Claude Fable 5 (50), Muse Spark 1.3 max (48) and GPT-5.6 Sol max (47); GLM-5.3-Flash (42) was the third open-weights model ({{Artificial Analysis|https://artificialanalysis.ai/articles/artificial-analysis-intelligence-index-v4-3}}). The same models scored 13 to 18 points lower than on v4.1.1, so scores from the three versions do not compare ([[chart|t-models|v-aaidx]]).

followups.t: A published design for recurrent looped transformers
followups.html: Yifan Zhang (Princeton) published the Recurrent Looped Transformer, a specification of the architecture family Astra is assumed to use: the decoder's hidden state and sliding-window cache carry across every token. It "explicitly reports no measured efficiency, reasoning quality, or scaling results" ({{MarkTechPost|https://www.marktechpost.com/2026/09/13/a-princeton-researcher-proposes-recurrent-looped-transformer-rlt/}}).

followups.t: Anthropic said to pick Nasdaq for its IPO
followups.html: Bloomberg reported that Anthropic chose Nasdaq for its listing (headline read; the article is paywalled), as carried in the {{2026-09-14 issue|n:3db5c17b0d0d8135a34af60966c5ecc1}}, which dates the choice Sep 9 and puts the target near $2 trillion. Timing was later reported as October or November.

The promised framework arrived with three review tracks and six reports from training and evaluation, among them a model that used an exposed API key found on GitHub and then fabricated nine figures, and one that uploaded retrieved records to a public paste service to cite them ({{MarkTechPost, Sep 17|https://www.marktechpost.com/2026/09/17/openai-releases-a-model-misalignment-disclosure-framework-with-3-review-tracks-and-6-incident-reports-from-rl-training/}}).

followups.t: AMD to buy World Labs for $8.2 billion
followups.html: AMD agreed to acquire World Labs, Atlas's maker, in an all-stock deal worth about $8.2 billion, pending regulatory approval; Fei-Fei Li becomes AMD's executive vice president and chief scientist ({{Tom's Hardware|https://www.tomshardware.com/tech-industry/artificial-intelligence/amd-acquires-ai-legend-fei-fei-lis-world-labs-for-usd8-2-billion-imagenet-pioneer-will-become-amd-chief-scientist-as-the-chipmaker-brings-her-lab-in-house}}).

followups.t: Google back in the top three
followups.html: Gemini 4 Argon (high) scored 53 on index v4.3, matching GPT-6 Astra (max), at $1.99 per task with a 50% launch discount, 60% of Astra's $3.26, or $3.98 once the discount ends ({{Artificial Analysis|https://artificialanalysis.ai/articles/gemini-4-argon-google-top-three-labs}}). Google had been seventh of the seven labs the issue lists.
